canonFrame.defaultEra: 836 PD, contemporary with Explorer's Guide to Wildemount and Tal'Dorei Campaign Setting Reborn
canonFrame.editionAssumptions: Use Explorer's Guide to Wildemount and Tal'Dorei Campaign Setting Reborn as the principal published setting layer. They describe overlapping years around Critical Role's second campaign. Do not automatically apply later streamed campaign outcomes, animated-series changes, or unpublished table lore.
canonFrame.timelineNotes: Exandria uses PD, Post-Divergence, for the modern calendar. The world was reshaped by the Calamity, after which the Prime Deities and Betrayer Gods were sealed beyond the Divine Gate. Published books may describe different continents at slightly different moments. Use 836 PD as a practical default and ask before incorporating major actual-play events.

campaignFoundations: Exandria is a whole world containing several continents, not only Tal'Dorei or Wildemount.
The Calamity destroyed most Age of Arcanum civilization and permanently scarred the world.
The Divine Gate prevents gods from physically entering the mortal world while allowing influence and divine magic.
Ancient magical ruins, divine battlefields, and lost artifacts remain active campaign forces.
Regional politics are morally complicated; no major state should be treated as an uncomplicated good faction.
Magic ranges from ordinary spellcraft to dunamancy, blood magic, divine relics, and Age of Arcanum technology.
The Cobalt Soul, Cerberus Assembly, Kryn Dynasty, Dwendalian Empire, Clovis Concord, and other factions have limited information and internal tensions.
Famous actual-play heroes exist only to the extent selected by the campaign.
The player characters are not required to repeat or serve Vox Machina, the Mighty Nein, or Bells Hells.
Local communities and cultures should remain distinct across continents.
gameMasterGuidance: Ask which published and streamed campaign events count before using famous outcomes.
Default to 836 PD and published setting books.
Use the Calamity as deep history and material consequence, not a reason every plot becomes divine apocalypse.
Keep gods behind the Divine Gate unless a campaign explicitly changes the cosmology.
Treat factions as internally divided and geographically limited.
Distinguish Tal'Dorei, Wildemount, Marquet, and Issylra culturally and politically.
Make relics and dunamancy rare enough to remain consequential.
Create original local NPCs, institutions, and conflicts that fit established regions.
Mark campaign-created lore separately from broadcast canon.
canonBoundaries: Do not merge the animated Legend of Vox Machina continuity with tabletop canon by default.
Do not assume every Critical Role campaign outcome has occurred.
Do not make the Divine Gate a complete barrier to divine magic or influence.
Do not make gods physically appear on Exandria in the modern era without exceptional circumstances.
Do not treat drow, goblinkin, or other Xhorhasian peoples as inherently evil.
Do not make the Kryn Dynasty, Dwendalian Empire, or Tal'Dorei Republic morally uniform.
Do not assume all Age of Arcanum ruins use the same magic or purpose.
Do not turn Vestiges of Divergence into ordinary magic items.
Do not make every Cobalt Soul archive omniscient.
When book and stream chronology differ, ask which continuity the player wants.

referenceChunks.title: History and Eras of Exandria
referenceChunks.text: Exandrian history is commonly divided into the Founding, the Age of Arcanum, the Calamity, and the modern Post-Divergence era. During the Founding, deities shaped the world and created or guided mortal peoples. A conflict over the primordials divided the gods. Those who defended mortal life became known as the Prime Deities, while those who opposed them became the Betrayer Gods. The Betrayers were imprisoned after the Schism. Mortal arcane power grew during the Age of Arcanum. Great cities flew, archmages manipulated life and death, and magical civilization reached heights that modern nations cannot reproduce. The mortal mage who became the Raven Queen replaced the previous god of death, proving that divine order could be challenged. Vespin Chloras's attempt to seize power from the Betrayer Gods helped release them. The resulting Calamity was a war involving gods, mortals, primordials, monsters, and devastating magic. Floating cities fell, landscapes were transformed, and roughly two-thirds of Exandria's population died according to common accounts. Vasselheim survived as a major continuity of civilization. The Prime Deities eventually defeated the Betrayers and withdrew behind the Divine Gate, creating the Divergence. Modern years are counted PD, Post-Divergence. Civilization rebuilt, but Calamity ruins, sealed powers, divine weapons, and magical scars remain. Do not treat ancient history as perfectly documented. Temples, states, and scholars preserve different narratives. A ruin can reveal that a celebrated Age of Arcanum city was exploitative or that a modern church simplified an old alliance. Historical uncertainty should invite discovery without erasing the established sequence.

referenceChunks.title: Gods and the Divine Gate
referenceChunks.editionScope: Explorer's Guide to Wildemount and Tal'Dorei Reborn
referenceChunks.text: Exandria's pantheon contains Prime Deities, Betrayer Gods, and lesser idols or powerful entities that receive worship. The Prime Deities include powers associated with knowledge, nature, civilization, change, craft, death, dawn, justice, and other domains. The Betrayers include tyrants, destroyers, corrupters, and imprisoned powers whose cults remain active. The Divine Gate prevents the gods themselves from physically entering the mortal world. It does not prevent prayer, visions, clerical magic, champions, celestials, fiends, dreams, relics, or indirect intervention. Divine actors therefore work through mortal institutions and agents. The Raven Queen was once mortal and ascended during the Age of Arcanum, replacing a prior death deity whose name was erased. Her history is both theological and political evidence that divinity can change. The Luxon is central to Kryn faith and dunamancy. Followers understand it through beacons, consecution, and the search for scattered light. Other theologians may not accept Kryn claims, and the Luxon's exact nature remains a mystery rather than a settled stat block. Worship varies by region. The Dwendalian Empire regulates approved gods. Vasselheim contains ancient temples and strong religious authority. Tal'Dorei and the Menagerie Coast maintain other balances. Betrayer cults can hide within legitimate institutions or survive around Calamity sites. Divine magic does not make a priest's political judgment correct. Temples contain sincere service, ambition, doctrine, local custom, and rivalry. Avoid having a god provide a complete answer when mortal action and interpretation are central to the campaign.

referenceChunks.title: Magic, Dunamancy, and Relics
referenceChunks.text: Modern Exandria supports familiar arcane and divine traditions alongside setting-specific magic. Dunamancy manipulates possibility, gravity, time, and related forces. It is strongly associated with the Kryn Dynasty and research into the Luxon, but knowledge can be stolen, shared, or independently developed. It should remain specialized and politically important. Vestiges of Divergence are legendary items created or empowered during the Calamity. Their power can awaken through deeds, personal growth, or extraordinary circumstances. Arms of the Betrayers are dangerous counterparts connected to fiends and Betrayer powers. Neither category should become a normal store inventory or a routine reward. Age of Arcanum ruins can contain advanced constructs, magical engines, weapons, laboratories, and systems whose purpose exceeds modern spellcasting. Aeor is a prominent fallen city beneath the ice of Eiselcross, but it is not the only ancient magical site. Different cities had different politics and technologies. Blood magic appears in traditions such as the Claret Orders and can be used for protection or predation. Hemocraft is morally contextual rather than automatically evil, though it carries physical and social costs. Magic affects travel, warfare, religion, trade, and status, but access is uneven. Skyships, teleportation, powerful healing, and resurrection depend on institutions and resources. When introducing a magical wonder, decide who controls it, what sustains it, and what old catastrophe or present rivalry surrounds it.

referenceChunks.title: Tal'Dorei
referenceChunks.text: Tal'Dorei is a continent west of Wildemount. Its central political power is the Republic of Tal'Dorei, formed after the fall of the tyrant Drassig line and later reshaped by crises associated with Vox Machina's era. The republic is represented through a council and connected settlements rather than exercising perfect control over the whole continent. Emon is the largest metropolis and political center, rebuilt after devastating attacks. Whitestone is an independent or closely allied city known for residuum, clockwork development, the de Rolo family, and recovery from occupation. Westruun, Kymal, Syngorn, Kraghammer, and other settlements have different governments and economies. The Ashari are elemental guardian communities associated with portals to the elemental planes. Their societies have local responsibilities and should not be reduced to wandering elemental monks. The Clasp and Myriad maintain criminal influence in parts of the continent. The Arcana Pansophical and Cobalt Soul connect scholarship and magical regulation to wider Exandria. Tal'Dorei contains deserts, forests, mountains, coasts, plains, ruins, fey crossings, and monster territories. The continent is not a continuous republic or a tour of Campaign 1 landmarks. Tal'Dorei Reborn is set roughly two decades after the beginning of Vox Machina's campaign and around the time of Campaign 2. If the party wants a world without Vox Machina's canonical achievements, use the original political foundations and create a different recent history. Otherwise, keep famous heroes mostly in the background.

referenceChunks.title: Emon and Central Tal'Dorei
referenceChunks.text: Emon is a large, cosmopolitan city on Tal'Dorei's western coast and the principal seat of the republic. It contains noble and wealthy districts, crowded commercial wards, temples, docks, entertainment, scholarship, criminal networks, and neighborhoods shaped by reconstruction. The city's past includes tyrannical rule, revolution, and catastrophic attack. Government through the Tal'Dorei Council distributes authority among representatives and specialists. Exact council membership is a timeline-sensitive published detail and need not be loaded into every campaign. The important operating fact is that Emon combines republican institutions with wealth, patronage, bureaucracy, and unequal influence. Cloudtop contains elite estates and high status. Other districts support trade, crafts, labor, migration, and vice. Famous establishments and NPCs can exist, but an original crew should know its own taverns, landlords, ward officials, and fixers. Reconstruction creates property disputes, memorial politics, public works, corruption, and generational differences. Older residents remember destruction; younger residents inherit stories and rebuilt streets. Residuum and magical commerce connect Emon to Whitestone and wider trade. Adventures can involve council intrigue, elemental threats, criminal competition, old tunnels, public festivals, magical regulation, or frontier pressure beyond the city. Do not have the council or a famous archmage solve every emergency. Emon works best when its democratic ideals create debate rather than effortless consensus.

referenceChunks.title: Wildemount
referenceChunks.text: Wildemount is divided into several broad regions. Western Wynandir contains the Dwendalian Empire, including the Zemni Fields and Marrow Valley. Eastern Wynandir is Xhorhas, much of it scarred during the Calamity and governed in large part by the Kryn Dynasty. The Menagerie Coast is a tropical trade region organized through the Clovis Concord. The Greying Wildlands contain independent settlements, criminal territories, forests, mountains, and northern frontiers. Eiselcross holds dangerous islands and Age of Arcanum ruins in the far north. At the default date, the Dwendalian Empire and Kryn Dynasty are at war in the published setting. A campaign can begin during that war, before it, or with a different outcome. Do not assume the streamed resolution unless selected. Wildemount's history includes the Calamity, the Julous Dominion, imperial expansion, the rise of the Cerberus Assembly, Kryn unification, coastal trade, and repeated struggles over ancient magic. The same ruin can be a military objective, sacred site, archaeological resource, and danger to nearby communities. Daily life differs sharply. Imperial citizens face regulated religion and state authority. Xhorhasian communities include many peoples treated as monsters elsewhere. Coastal city-states emphasize trade and local autonomy. Northern settlements may depend on clans, crime families, mines, hunters, or isolation. When a character says they are from Wildemount, narrow the answer to a region, nation, and community. Accent, food, faith, law, and assumptions about monsters should follow that choice.

referenceChunks.title: The Dwendalian Empire
referenceChunks.text: The Dwendalian Empire controls much of western Wynandir from Rexxentrum. King Bertrand Dwendal rules through monarchy, nobles, military forces, bureaucracy, controlled faith, and the uneasy support of the Cerberus Assembly. The empire offers roads, law, markets, military security, and civic identity while suppressing dissent and regulating information. The Crownsguard and Righteous Brand serve policing and military functions. Local officials, nobles, guilds, and temples interpret imperial policy unevenly. Approved worship is regulated, and gods associated with dangerous or disfavored powers may be illegal. This creates private faith, smuggling, selective enforcement, and sincere support for order. Rexxentrum is a wealthy capital of court, administration, arcane institutions, temples, and inequality. Zadash is another major city with commercial, military, and religious importance. Rural villages and provincial towns experience imperial power differently from the capital. The Cerberus Assembly is a coalition of powerful mages bound to the crown after earlier arcane conflict. It supports education, research, war, and state power while pursuing internal rivalries and secret projects. It is not perfectly controlled by the king and is not one unified villain. During war with the Kryn Dynasty, propaganda portrays Xhorhasian peoples as monsters and frames security measures as necessity. Characters can encounter genuine enemy operations, fabricated threats, and opportunistic officials. Avoid making every imperial citizen complicit at the same level; show how institutions convert fear and ordinary loyalty into power.

referenceChunks.title: The Kryn Dynasty and Xhorhas
referenceChunks.text: The Kryn Dynasty is centered in Rosohna, formerly Ghor Dranas, an ancient stronghold associated with the Betrayer Gods. Drow who escaped Lolth's control embraced the Luxon and built a surface civilization that incorporated many peoples of Xhorhas, including goblinkin, orcs, humans, minotaurs, and others. Luxon beacons are sacred objects and sources of dunamantic study. Through consecution, specially prepared souls can be reborn near a beacon and later recover memories of prior lives. This creates long-lived political continuity among the consecuted and difficult questions about identity, status, memory, and power. Not every Kryn citizen is consecuted or a dunamancer. The Bright Queen Leylas Kryn is the dynasty's long-serving ruler in the published default. The Aurora Watch provides military security. Dens and noble structures organize influence. The Children of Malice and other agents of Lolth oppose Kryn religious and political order. Xhorhas is environmentally varied despite its reputation as a blasted waste. The Calamity left dangerous monsters, ruins, and scarred landscapes, but communities farm, trade, celebrate, and govern. Permanent magical darkness in major areas is a political and cultural adaptation, not proof that residents cannot tolerate daylight universally. The war with the Dwendalian Empire involves stolen beacons, borders, propaganda, and older fear. Do not portray the Kryn as automatically enlightened. Consecution can support hierarchy, the dynasty expands influence, and internal dissent exists. Its importance is that peoples called monsters elsewhere possess a complex state with its own virtues and failures.

referenceChunks.title: The Menagerie Coast
referenceChunks.text: The Menagerie Coast is a tropical region of ports, jungles, islands, trade routes, and independent city-states. The Clovis Concord coordinates major cities through marquises and commercial agreements. It is a coalition, not a unified nation with one bureaucracy. Port Damali is the largest city and a major center of commerce, shipping, wealth, crime, and political influence. Nicodranas is another important port with cultural and diplomatic connections. Smaller communities depend on fishing, plantations, crafts, inland resources, and sea trade. The Revelry is a pirate confederation and maritime threat with political and economic motives. The Myriad and other criminal groups compete within coastal cities. Corruption can involve tariffs, port appointments, cargo insurance, private security, and selective anti-piracy campaigns. The coast's beauty should not erase danger or inequality. Jungles contain ancient sites, monsters, and local communities. Ocean routes face storms, sea creatures, pirates, and foreign powers. Wealthy districts, resorts, and markets depend on dock labor, sailors, farmers, and transport. The Clovis Concord is formally neutral in the war between the Empire and Dynasty but profits, spies, negotiates, and fears disruption. A campaign can focus on maritime exploration, political bargaining, smuggling, archaeology, tourism, or local defense. Distinguish individual cities rather than treating the coast as one festival beach.

referenceChunks.title: The Greying Wildlands and Eiselcross
referenceChunks.text: The Greying Wildlands lie north of the great powers and contain forests, mountains, tundra, mines, isolated settlements, and territories outside strong centralized government. Shadycreek Run is influenced by competing crime families and serves fugitives, merchants, and dangerous enterprises. It should not be portrayed as having no social order; family power, deals, and reputation substitute for stable public law. Uthodurn is an underground city governed through a dwarven and elven diarchy. It emerged from cooperation between displaced peoples and developed distinctive craft, politics, and relations with surrounding lands. Other northern communities include hunters, firbolgs, goliaths, dwarves, elves, and mixed settlements. Eiselcross is an island region in the far north containing ruins of Aeor and other Age of Arcanum sites. Expeditions face cold, magical anomalies, rival researchers, monsters, unstable relics, and logistical limits. Balenpost and similar bases support exploration and competition. Aeor was a powerful flying city opposed to the gods before its fall during the Calamity. Its ruins include advanced magic and evidence of ethically dangerous research. Do not make every Aeorian discovery a weapon intended to kill gods; cities require food, transit, housing, medicine, records, and ordinary infrastructure. Northern campaigns should make weather and distance meaningful while preserving politics. Salvage rights, academic ethics, supply, indigenous knowledge, and who controls recovered magic matter as much as surviving a ruin.

referenceChunks.title: Marquet and Ank'Harel
referenceChunks.editionScope: Call of the Netherdeep and published Exandria lore
referenceChunks.text: Marquet is a continent containing deserts, mountains, coasts, jungles, cities, trade routes, and cultures beyond the limited areas described in early publications. Ank'Harel, the Jewel of Hope, is a major desert metropolis built around water, commerce, scholarship, temples, entertainment, and political power. Ank'Harel is traditionally associated with the rule of J'mon Sa Ord, an ancient brass dragon who usually appears in mortal form. The Hands of Ord enforce law and security. The Allegiance of Allsight studies history and magic. The Consortium of the Vermilion Dream seeks powerful supernatural knowledge through less restrained methods. The Cobalt Soul maintains a presence. Districts differ in wealth, function, architecture, and access to water. Markets connect Marquet to Tal'Dorei, Wildemount, and other lands. Desert travel depends on routes, guides, mounts, weather, and local relationships. Published actual-play material later explores additional Marquet locations and political changes. Do not import those events or a fully mapped continent unless the campaign selects them. Avoid representing Marquet solely through desert stereotypes; choose a specific city, people, and environment. Ank'Harel supports archaeology, faction competition, urban mystery, planar danger, art, and diplomacy. Its order is real but not omniscient. A dragon ruler does not personally decide every permit or investigate every crime. Local officials, scholars, merchants, neighborhoods, and criminal groups should carry daily play.

referenceChunks.title: Issylra and Vasselheim
referenceChunks.text: Issylra is the continent containing Vasselheim, the Dawn City, widely regarded as Exandria's oldest surviving city. Vasselheim endured the Calamity and holds ancient temples, archives, orders, fortifications, and traditions connected to the Prime Deities. Religious districts and institutions wield major influence. The city has hosted the Cobalt Soul and numerous orders, warriors, priests, and scholars. Its claim to sacred continuity can produce conservatism, genuine preservation, rivalry among temples, and political authority. Beyond Vasselheim, Issylra includes diverse wilderness and communities less fully described in principal sourcebooks. Do not treat the whole continent as empty land surrounding one holy city. When moving beyond published detail, establish campaign-created cultures carefully and avoid presenting them as canonical. Vasselheim's defenses and religious power do not make it safe from internal conflict. Relics, forbidden cults, doctrinal disputes, pilgrims, refugees, and ancient sealed sites provide adventure. Officials may fear another Calamity enough to suppress risky knowledge. The city is a useful setting for questions about who owns history. A temple may hold an artifact recovered elsewhere. The Cobalt Soul may seek evidence a church considers dangerous. A foreign worshipper may find their practice treated as improper. Use institutional memory as both a protection and a source of power.

referenceChunks.title: Factions and Networks
referenceChunks.text: The Library of the Cobalt Soul serves Ioun through scholarship, archives, investigation, and efforts to expose corruption. Expositors act as specialized field agents. The organization operates across continents, but archives and chapters do not share perfect knowledge. The Cerberus Assembly is a powerful coalition of mages within the Dwendalian Empire. Members control schools, research, state projects, and personal networks while competing with one another. The Myriad is a criminal organization with cells, fronts, and shifting relationships. The Clasp is especially associated with Tal'Dorei. The Claret Orders use blood magic and monster-hunting traditions. The Golden Grin is a loose network opposing tyranny through humor, performance, information, and direct action. The Arcana Pansophical gathers powerful mages around rules concerning dangerous magic. The Ashari guard elemental portals through separate communities. Factions should enter through local representatives, not omniscient headquarters. An agent may have incomplete orders, personal loyalties, and a rival inside the same organization. Membership provides contacts and obligations, not universal access. Avoid using faction alignment as a substitute for motive. The Cobalt Soul can hoard knowledge, the Golden Grin can be reckless, the Assembly can produce useful scholarship, and a criminal network can protect a neighborhood while exploiting it. Preserve canonical goals while allowing institutional contradiction.

referenceChunks.title: Cultures, Calendar, and Moons
referenceChunks.text: Modern Exandrian dates use Post-Divergence reckoning. Regional calendars share broad structures but can differ in holidays, names, and religious observance. Use the selected sourcebook's local calendar when exact dates matter rather than inventing a universal format. Exandria has two moons: Catha, the larger familiar moon, and Ruidus, the smaller red moon. Ruidus is associated with superstition, unusual births, omens, and mysteries. Later actual-play campaigns greatly expand its lore. Do not import those revelations into an 836 PD campaign unless selected. Ordinary people can hold conflicting beliefs without knowing cosmic truth. Languages, ancestry, and culture are not identical. The Kryn Dynasty includes many ancestries under one political order. Tal'Dorei cities contain migrants from several continents. Coastal trade mixes communities. A character's homeland, class, faith, and family should shape them more than a generic species template. Goblinkin, orcs, drow, minotaurs, and other peoples may be treated as monsters by imperial or traditional narratives while living ordinary social lives elsewhere. Do not reproduce that propaganda as objective setting truth. Use food, manners, clothing, music, architecture, public institutions, and attitudes toward magic to distinguish regions. Avoid heavy phonetic accents. When published lore is thin, mark new cultural detail as campaign-created rather than presenting it as something said on stream.

referenceChunks.title: Common Exandria Canon Traps
referenceChunks.text: The greatest trap is assuming all viewers' knowledge forms one synchronized canon. Explorer's Guide to Wildemount, Tal'Dorei Reborn, Call of the Netherdeep, streamed campaigns, comics, novels, and animation can occupy different dates or continuities. Ask which sources count. Do not insert famous player characters into every crisis. Their existence does not make them available, informed, or responsible for the party. Avoid recreating streamed plots by default. The Divine Gate blocks physical divine entry, not divine magic. The Calamity is past but materially present through ruins and scars. Vestiges are legendary, not common. Dunamancy is specialized, not a universal school taught in every academy. The Dwendalian Empire is authoritarian without every citizen being evil. The Kryn Dynasty offers a refuge from some prejudices without being flawless. The Clovis Concord is a coalition, not one nation. Xhorhas is not an empty monster wasteland. Do not merge animated-series alterations into tabletop history automatically. Do not reveal later Ruidus or Campaign 3 lore in an 836 PD game unless the player requests it. When exact published information is absent, create local lore openly as campaign canon. Exandria invites new stories; accuracy means knowing which details are established and which belong to this table.
